analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to guarantee specialist access, disclose costs, end doctor gag clauses, and hear patient appeals.
analysis.headline: Backed by 12 House members of both parties, the bill never left House subcommittees and died without a vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced HMOs and other managed care plans to guarantee patients timely access to specialists, ban bonuses that pay doctors for limiting care, void contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients their full treatment options, and create expedited appeal boards for denied claims, including boards with independent medical experts. It also would have required plans to disclose premiums, denial rates, and financial incentives annually so patients could compare them. Its strongest access option — letting enrollees buy out-of-network care — was deferred until at least 2002 and only if a federal study found the other protections failed.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients enrolled in managed care plans, especially those fighting denials of specialist care or chronic-condition treatment. They would gain guaranteed timely access to appropriate specialists, continuity of care for chronic conditions, expedited grievance procedures, appeal boards staffed with medical experts who have no financial stake in the plan, and annual disclosure of plan costs, denial-reversal rates, and doctor-payment incentives. Doctors would also gain, since the bill voids gag clauses and bans payments designed to induce doctors to withhold medically necessary care.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees enrollees in plans that restrict provider choice timely access to primary and specialty care appropriate to their condition, including direct access to specialists for ongoing care of chronic conditions.

Bans plans from paying doctors, directly or indirectly, as an inducement to reduce or limit medically necessary services, and voids any contract clause prohibiting doctors from telling patients how physicians are paid, what utilization-review rules are, what drugs are on the formulary, or what their treatment options are.

Creates a meaningful, expedited grievance process with timely written notice of every denial and its reasons, and requires each plan to convene an appeals board within 30 days that includes consumer members and independent medical experts with no financial interest in the plan.

Requires plans to give enrollees an annual, comparable information checklist covering premiums, deductibles, network doctors, utilization-control incentives, and the percentage of coverage requests denied and later reversed, so patients can judge plans before and after enrolling.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care companies would bear the compliance costs of new access guarantees, appeals boards, gag-clause removal, and detailed public disclosure. Employers that sponsor group health plans would share those costs, and the bill itself directs a federal study of any resulting premium increases; some cost would likely flow to employers and enrollees through premiums.

drawbacks.text: The new mandates impose real compliance costs on plans and employers, and the bill itself requires a study of 'any additional costs imposed,' implicitly acknowledging that premiums or employer costs could rise.

The bill's strongest access provision — requiring plans to offer an out-of-network coverage option — would not take effect until 2002 at the earliest, and only if the HHS Secretary found patients were not getting quality care and Congress agreed by law or joint resolution.

Imposing federal requirements on every employer plan covered by ERISA could lead some employers to scale back benefits or shift costs to offset the added expense — the standard good-faith objection to any insurance mandate, which is why the bill built in a transition for collectively bargained plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address documented, concrete harms of 1990s managed care — restricted specialist access, doctor gag clauses, bonuses for limiting care, and opaque denials — and the appeal and disclosure provisions give patients real tools. The costs are compliance burdens and possible modest premium increases, which the bill chose to study rather than cap. The design is cautious rather than radical: the out-of-network option, its costliest feature, is gated behind a federal study and congressional action. On balance the benefits to patients outweigh the acknowledged costs, though the deferral of the out-of-network provision makes the bill weaker than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House subcommittees from April 1998 onward; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Weldon introduced the bill on March 25, 1998 with five original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Ted Strickland of Ohio and Republicans Tom Coburn of Oklahoma and John Cooksey of Mississippi.
Eleven members cosponsored the bill in total — 7 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

The Speaker referred it to two committees, Commerce and Education and the Workforce; it went to the Commerce Health and Environment Subcommittee on March 31, 1998 and the Education and Workforce Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on April 17, 1998.
No further action of any kind was taken; the April 17 subcommittee referral was the bill's last action, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and the employers who sponsor health plans are better off, because they avoided the access, disclosure, and appeals mandates for at least another Congress. Patients in restrictive plans gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with 7 Democratic, 3 Republican, and 1 Independent cosponsors — but no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so no vote splits exist to measure the parties.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care organizations (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would bar the core managed care cost-control tools of the era: bonuses to doctors for limiting care, contract gag clauses, unexplained denials, and restricted specialist access, and would force public disclosure of denial rates. Insurers' savings from those tools came directly at patients' expense, so their interest ran against the bill's beneficiaries.

Doctors would be freed from contract clauses restricting what they may tell patients and from payment structures that penalize referrals and necessary treatment, and independent physicians would sit on plan appeal boards.
Employers would absorb compliance costs for the new guarantees, disclosure, and appeals boards, likely through higher premiums — though their employees are the patients who benefit.
